## Environment

## Minimal steps

Per-scenario matrix. "Verdict" classifies against current main, where the access token is never checked in the request path (only the client-invoked /api/oauth/validate), so on main an OIDC session simply lives for the 21-day cookie regardless of token expiry or IdP revocation. Keycloak realm event log (LOGIN, CODE_TO_TOKEN, REFRESH_TOKEN, REFRESH_TOKEN_ERROR) used as ground truth for how many token-endpoint calls actually happened.

| # | Scenario | Observed outcome | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Access token expires mid-session, next request | Refreshed in place, request returned 200, session survived | REFRESH_TOKEN event at IdP exactly when the first post-expiry request landed | Improvement, works as claimed |
| 2 | Rotation: is the new refresh token stored and usable? | Second post-expiry cycle also 200; two REFRESH_TOKEN successes, zero errors. Rotated token was stored and reused correctly. Piggybacked (coalesced) requests also received usable rotated tokens via the snapshot copy | IdP event log; follow-up request on a racer jar succeeded | Improvement, the classic keep-the-old-token bug is absent |
| 3a | 8 parallel requests with the same cookies at expiry | All 8 returned 200; exactly one REFRESH_TOKEN event. Coalescing works | IdP event log: single refresh for the burst | Improvement, works as claimed |
| 3b | Near-miss race: stale-cookie request arriving after the in-flight refresh finished (fired at +40ms) | invalid_grant, forced logout; subsequent requests on the same trilium.sid die instantly (401 in 2ms). One losing near-miss racer kills the whole session. The in-flight map entry is deleted when the token-endpoint call resolves, not when the initiating response (with Set-Cookie) reaches the client, so the unprotected window is handler time plus response latency; wider on slow endpoints or high-RTT links. Keycloak reuse detection additionally revokes the whole token family, so even the freshly rotated tokens die | A=200 t=18ms, B(+40ms)=401 with REFRESH_TOKEN_ERROR at IdP, C(+80ms)/D(+150ms)=401 t=2ms; trilium log "OIDC refresh token rejected by IdP (invalid_grant)... Forcing re-authentication" | New failure mode vs main (main never kills the session); mitigated by coalescing for truly concurrent bursts; residual window is narrow locally but real. Worth a maintainer look; not a blocker if invalid_grant-is-terminal is the intended policy |
| 4a | Refresh token revoked at IdP (admin logout + consent revoke), next request after expiry | Graceful: 401 in 22ms, no 500, no hang; clean log line; /login redirects into re-auth | after_revoke=401 t=0.022s; trilium.log invalid_grant line | Improvement (main would never notice revocation) |
| 4b | IdP outage (container paused) at expiry | Request stalled the full oauthHttpTimeout (30.0s) then returned 200 with the expired token; log "OIDC token refresh failed: operation timed out. Continuing with the expired access token."; session survived and refreshed normally after the outage | during_outage=200 real 0m30.017s | Acceptable degradation; the 30s per-session stall is the cost of the fail-open choice; 30s timeout default is pre-existing |
| 5 | offline_access opt-in semantics vs a standards-compliant provider | With scope lacking offline_access, Keycloak still issues a session-bound (type "Refresh") token and the middleware actively refreshes with it: REFRESH_TOKEN event observed post-expiry, request 200. The code comment's assumption ("no refresh token is present... the common case, and a no-op here") does not hold for Keycloak-family providers | IdP event log shows refresh_token_type Refresh (vs Offline with opt-in); noscope_after_expiry=200 | Behavior change even without opt-in: once the SSO idle timeout (Keycloak default 30 min) lapses, refresh hits invalid_grant and the session is forced to re-auth, where main kept its local 21-day session. Arguably correct SSO behavior, but it is not the no-op the comment claims, and maintainers should know idle sessions now end at the IdP idle timeout |

Google specifics (code reading, not live-tested): strips offline_access from the scope, sends access_type=offline plus prompt=consent, client_secret_post; consistent with Google documented behavior; non-rotating providers are handled naturally since a missing refresh_token in the refresh response leaves the stored one in place. Live verification would need a real Google client.

## Expected

PR claims: in-place refresh on expiry, rotation-safe storage of the new refresh token, coalesced concurrent refreshes, terminal invalid_grant handling, fail-open on transient errors, per-issuer offline-access opt-in.

## Actual

All headline claims verified live (scenarios 1, 2, 3a, 4a, 4b). Two findings that change the picture: the near-miss race window after a completed refresh force-kills the whole session under rotation (3b), and the middleware is not a no-op without offline_access on providers that always issue refresh tokens (5), which shortens idle sessions to the IdP SSO idle timeout.
